Multimodal lectures with visual aids like slides, hand-written notes, and body language are more engaging than single-channel videos, making them ideal for knowledge transfer. However, creating such presentations manually is time-consuming and prone to errors. Existing studies on multimodal lecture generation have focused on individual modalities or produced generic content without considering the specific generation needs of the end-user. To address these limitations, we propose an innovative framework that leverages the skills of multiple experts - a slide generation model, a text-to-video model, and a body language generation model - to produce high-quality multimodal videos tailored to specific users and conversation topics. Our approach is evaluated through both automated and human assessments on two real-world tasks: generating videos for educational lectures and creating product demonstration videos. The results demonstrate that our multimodal generation pipeline significantly outperforms existing single-modal video generation models in both tasks. Our research also proposes a new method for integrating surprasital and reading time data to better understand the processing priorities of language models. This paper presents a novel approach to defining an optimal control problem, where the final state is confined to a set of n-1 co-dimensions. By integrating dynamic programming principles with set-valued analysis, we develop a non-smooth maximum principle, which is demonstrated to be applicable to problems involving control systems with n-1 co-dimensions. Our theory's effectiveness is illustrated through the resolution of a classic optimal problem, a cart mass problem, using both analytical and numerical methods. Furthermore, we establish that our maximum principle converges to the traditional Pontryagin maximum principle as the co-dimension of the target set diminishes to one. Lastly, we extend the dynamic programming equation to accommodate problems with non-convex target sets, resulting in a semi-definite program formulation. Our findings are accompanied by numerical examples that illustrate the efficacy of the proposed methods. All accompanying code is provided for reproducibility. Training neural networks on long temporal data poses a significant challenge due to the inefficient use of backpropagation through time, which often results in a significant increase in computational requirements as the look-ahead period grows. To mitigate this issue, we introduce a novel approach called Skip-Sideways, which leverages a random skip architecture to only process future information that is available in the batch. By selectively skipping over input features, Skip-Sideways enables the efficient training of neural networks on long sequences, while maintaining comparable performance to the traditional backpropagation through time method. In addition, we provide a theoretical analysis of Skip-Sideways, which explains its empirical benefits and identifies the optimal configuration for achieving high performance. Our extensive experiments on multiple temporal sequence tasks demonstrate the superior efficacy of Skip-Sideways, especially when working with long sequences. We present simplified and broadened versions of the Chernoff bound, specifically
informed by its applications within the field of concentration theory. The revised
Chernoff bounds are achieved by combining the use of moment generating functions
with recent advancements in the union bound over subsets. The new inequalities 
outperform the original Chernoff bound and are also more efficient in terms of 
computational requirements, particularly requiring less time to calculate. The 
algorithms for these new inequalities have been made publicly available in Python. 
Additionally, we demonstrate the effectiveness of these new Chernoff bounds by 
applying them to a problem in online learning. Specifically, we utilize them to 
derive an upper bound on the regret of an online learning algorithm known as 
exp3, thereby providing a tighter analysis compared to existing methods. The 
results of our analysis are further validated through experiments. The relevant 
code can be found at https://github.com/asharlet/Chernoff. We also provide a 
complementary Julia package for these new Chernoff bounds.

We've developed a method to assess how relevant a summary or definition is to an entity's name. This name relevance evaluation can be a valuable tool for several purposes: First, it allows us to identify whether an entity's summary accurately reflects its title. Second, it enables us to compare how well different summaries capture an entity's name. Finally, it empowers us to compare how effectively various summarization models generate text. The results of our experiments demonstrate that our model outperforms a baseline model and achieves high accuracy in evaluating the name relevance of summaries. We introduce a novel, adaptive algorithm called DART, designed to address the multi-armed bandit problem in a distributed setting. DART enables independent agents to collaboratively select the most promising arm from a shared pool of options, achieving an optimal regret of $O(\log t + \sqrt{t} \cdot \sqrt{\frac{|A| - 1}{|I|}})$ after $t$ rounds. DART's architecture is based on a decentralized approach, where agents form temporary clusters for information sharing, and the algorithm's regret is influenced by the number of participating agents, the number of available arms, and the size of each temporary cluster. The ability to query and analyze multimedia databases is crucial for extracting valuable insights, but traditional query languages often overlook the connections between various multimedia elements across different dimensions, such as time, color, and texture. This paper introduces a new query language called MMQL that allows users to express queries across multiple dimensions, enabling the discovery of complex relationships between various multimedia features. MMQL's query language is formally defined through an abstract syntax and semantic meaning, encompassing diverse query types including equality, range, temporal, spatial, feature, and logical queries. The paper also presents an optimization technique that reorders filters to minimize disk usage, along with an implementation of MMQL in a multimedia repository and an evaluation of its performance using real-world data. The results demonstrate MMQL's ability to efficiently manage multimedia databases, outperforming existing query languages in terms of processing speed. The paper concludes by highlighting the benefits of MMQL in facilitating the development of innovative multimedia applications. A comprehensive description of the MMQL language, including formal definitions and examples, is available in a supplementary document. Entity Linking datasets often rely on outdated Wikipedia data from 2016 and earlier, which is no longer suitable for state-of-the-art pre-trained language models due to their limited domain. To address this limitation, we introduce WikiGUM, a novel Entity Linking dataset based on the Goodfellow Unified Wikipedia snapshot from 2020. WikiGUM is a comprehensive collection of 1.5 million labeled pairs, derived from 15K sentences within 5K entities. We establish a baseline benchmark and conduct an in-depth analysis of the dataset, as well as experiments comparing state-of-the-art Entity Linking models trained on previous datasets, ultimately revealing that WikiGUM outperforms existing datasets and highlights the need for more recent and diverse data for modern NLP applications. Reasoning within associativity and commutativity often necessitates breaking down expressions into fundamental components, a process referred to as atomicity. Traditional methods for automated reasoning systems struggle with this task due to the exponential growth of possible atomicity choices, resulting in significant time and space requirements. This paper presents novel techniques to overcome these challenges, enabling the efficient identification of optimal choices and their corresponding proofs. Furthermore, we demonstrate the applicability of these advancements to a broader range of mathematical domains. Experimental results confirm a substantial improvement in performance compared to existing methods. Specifically, our approach can efficiently determine optimal choices for expressions with up to 15 variables within a reasonable timeframe, a feat previously unattainable. This achievement not only facilitates the automated verification of mathematical formulas but also supports the analysis of higher-level programming concepts, such as higher-order functional programming. All associated code and data are publicly accessible at https://github.com/hoangkdej/atomicity-choice. A companion video showcasing our experimental findings is available at https://youtu.be/6kQ6kQ6kQ6kQ. This research is a continuation of our earlier work presented at IJCAR 2020, and we have successfully addressed the identified issues, resulting in a substantial performance improvement. Moreover, our system is now capable of handling a broader range of mathematical domains. This paper is submitted to the journal Logical Methods in Artificial Intelligence, and we are grateful to the editors for their support. We also extend our gratitude to the reviewers for their thoughtful comments, contributing to the paper's improvement. Finally, we would like to express our appreciation to the workshop organizers of FoSSACS 2022 for providing the opportunity to present this work. The paper's content is entirely self-contained and can be understood without prior knowledge of our earlier work. The exponential growth in the amount of available information has created a significant challenge for information retrieval, particularly in the realm of scientific studies. Researchers are now faced with an overwhelming number of publications, making it difficult to locate and evaluate the most relevant research results from around the world related to their work. To address this issue, we have developed a cutting-edge information retrieval system that aggregates relevant scientific literature to support the planning and execution of experiments in the field of physics. By combining data from various sources, including PubMed, Scopus, and Google Scholar, our system provides users with a comprehensive overview of existing research in a specific area, as well as relevant studies that have explored similar research questions. To validate the effectiveness of our approach, we conducted a comprehensive evaluation involving 12 researchers from multiple institutions, which demonstrated that our method outperforms traditional search engines in assisting users to identify relevant research results. The results of our evaluation showed that users were able to locate relevant research faster and with greater precision when using our system compared to a conventional search engine. To further enhance the utility of our approach, we have made the source code available under an open-source license, allowing other researchers to adapt and extend our methodology to support the planning and execution of experiments in their own work. By doing so, we aim to provide a valuable resource that can facilitate the scientific community's access to relevant research results and support the development of innovative solutions to complex scientific challenges. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first study to develop a comprehensive information retrieval system that can assist users in locating relevant research results from across the globe. The integration of Augmented Reality (AR) technology with 5G and advanced wireless networks has given rise to a new class of mobile AR applications, which enable immersive experiences and efficient interactions. However, the high data traffic and resource-intensive processing in these applications can lead to significant energy consumption, which is particularly problematic for battery-limited mobile devices. To address this challenge, this study explores the potential of the 6G network's edge capabilities in enhancing the performance of mobile AR applications, specifically by offloading computationally intensive tasks to the edge environment. A novel framework is proposed to optimize edge resource allocation and user scheduling, which is designed to minimize energy consumption while ensuring real-time task completion. The framework's effectiveness is evaluated through simulations under various scenarios, including real-time and non-real-time settings, with results demonstrating a 25% reduction in energy consumption compared to a baseline approach. The simulations also reveal that the non-real-time scenario is more suitable for edge-edge computing, with a 10-fold increase in energy savings compared to the real-time scenario. These findings provide valuable insights for the development of edge-edge computing technologies in the 6G network. The phenomenon of over-parameterization in machine learning has been observed to enable neural networks to memorize random data, even while maintaining generalization to unseen data. Despite its implications, the underlying mechanism of this generalization capability remains unclear. This study aims to shed light on this process by analyzing the generalization behavior of linear models within the context of over-parameterization. By employing a random feature model, we investigate the effects of over-parameterization on generalization, specifically focusing on the bias-variance trade-off that arises from gradient descent optimization. Our findings indicate that the optimized solution converges to a critical point within the model's parameter space, exhibiting a unique balance between the solution's proximity to the true model and its distance from the model's minimum. This discovery provides a theoretical basis for the observed generalization capabilities of over-parameterized neural networks. Additionally, our study reveals that the generalization performance of these networks is influenced by the inherent geometry of the model parameter space, specifically the presence of symmetries and the effects of over-parameterization on the model's manifold. This insight has significant implications for the design of future machine learning models. Finally, our analysis is supported by numerical experiments that demonstrate the empirical implications of our theoretical findings. These experiments also reveal the potential benefits of over-parameterization in enhancing the robustness of neural networks to adversarial attacks. Furthermore, we observe that entanglement between particles can be leveraged to accelerate the evolution of composite systems, thereby violating the established speed limits. In this research, we introduce a novel approach to fake news detection, leveraging the strengths of both traditional and modern text analysis methods. By combining these techniques, we aim to enhance the accuracy of fake news detection, particularly in cases where biased language is used. Our proposed model, which integrates sentiment analysis with attention mechanisms, can effectively identify and downplay biased content, ultimately improving the detection of false news related to the COVID-19 pandemic. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of our model, achieving higher F1-scores compared to existing methods on a publicly available dataset. Furthermore, our ablation studies confirm the effectiveness of attention mechanisms in enhancing the performance of fake news detection systems. This is achieved by developing a novel loss function that encourages the models to be robust against a wide range of attacks, which are generated by a diverse set of generators. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach outperforms existing methods in various scenarios, showcasing its effectiveness in enhancing model robustness. The Weierstrass sigma function, a periodic meromorphic function of two variables, is a fundamental component in the Riemann theta function, a doubly periodic holomorphic function, when expressed as an elliptic theta function. By leveraging the properties of the theta function, we have devised a novel method to compute the Weierstrass sigma function, allowing us to derive its second-order derivatives at the lattice points without relying on the existing complicated algorithm. Furthermore, we have developed an algorithm to compute the Weierstrass zeta function, a crucial component in the function's asymptotic expansion, at the lattice points by leveraging the Weierstrass sigma function and its second-order derivatives. The new approach significantly simplifies the computation of these functions, making it more efficient compared to the previously established methods. The proposed algorithms have been implemented in the Singular interface for the computation of Weierstrass sigma function and zeta function, and their efficacy has been demonstrated through the computation of numerous examples. The results indicate that our algorithm outperforms the existing algorithm developed by Eberard in terms of computational efficiency. This approach enables the integration of multiple tasks into a single neural network, where each task is represented by a distinct frequency channel. Through the application of STDP rules, researchers have demonstrated the ability to multiplex information across channels, a skill that can be further optimized by strategically modifying the STDP rules. By applying this learning mechanism to tasks such as delayed echo state networks and reservoir computing, researchers have successfully created a neural network capable of multiplexing multiple tasks, a skill that has been validated through extensive simulations. The results of this study hold significant implications for the development of advanced neural networks and machine learning algorithms. Furthermore, this work provides a valuable framework for exploring the brain's ability to multiplex information and for developing innovative solutions to complex problem-solving challenges. Ultimately, this research aims to facilitate the development of more reliable and efficient multi-site rsfMRI studies. Complex systems such as weather forecasting, traffic flow, and stock market trends generate vast amounts of spatial-temporal data. This data often lacks labels, and extracting meaningful information from it is a significant challenge. To address this issue, we propose a novel approach that combines a probabilistic model with a neural network's capabilities. Our method, based on the Bregman divergence, can effectively manage spatial and temporal relationships within the data. Utilizing the Expectation-Maximization algorithm, we derive a probabilistic model that can be integrated with neural networks to predict missing data. Through theoretical analysis and experimental validation on both artificial and real-world datasets, we demonstrate the superior performance of our proposed method in comparison to existing algorithms. Our approach's flexibility and applicability make it a valuable tool for tackling complex spatial-temporal problems. A key challenge in training generative models with adversarial networks is mode collapse, which occurs when the network converges to a limited set of output possibilities. In this study, we examine mode collapse in generative adversarial networks by analyzing the underlying dynamics using a second-order approximation of the network's loss function. Our approach reveals that the critical issue lies in the interaction between the network and its loss function, specifically the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the loss function's Hessian. We demonstrate that the eigenvalues of the Hessian dictate the long-term behavior of the network, and the eigenvectors indicate the directions of its internal modes. Furthermore, we show that the network's internal dynamics are influenced by the presence of saddle points, which can lead to mode collapse. Our theoretical findings are supported by numerical simulations, which confirm the effectiveness of our approach in preventing mode collapse in generative adversarial networks. The results of this study are expected to contribute to the development of more effective generative models. The use of dynamic nuclear polarization (DNP) is a highly effective technique for increasing the sensitivity of nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) experiments, particularly in systems with limited spin density. Diamond's unique properties make it an ideal candidate for DNP studies, as it contains both $^{13}$C and $^{14}$N nuclei, which can be polarized using electron spin resonance (ESR) methods. This research focuses on optimizing DNP in bulk $^{13}$C diamond samples, exploring various parameters such as irradiation power, temperature, and DNP agent concentration. The results demonstrate that microwave power plays a crucial role in DNP, with optimal power levels exceeding those typically used in NMR experiments, resulting in significant hyperpolarization enhancements of up to 80 times the bulk magnetization. Additionally, this study examines the effects of diamond powder particle size and surface treatment on DNP, revealing notable enhancements for smaller particles and treated samples, particularly when combined with optimal microwave power levels. The findings of this research provide valuable insights for the development of DNP-enhanced NMR experiments in bulk diamond systems. Furthermore, this study demonstrates the potential for DNP-enhanced NMR to detect and analyze diamond's surface-adsorbed compounds, as illustrated by the successful detection of a small amount of nitroso group ($^{14}$N=O) in a nitrogen-vacancy-doped diamond sample. The results of this research are expected to contribute significantly to the advancement of diamond-based quantum computing and sensing applications. However, the sampling matrix associated with this grid is non-orthogonal, making it difficult to apply certain established techniques for signal reconstruction. In this paper, we present a novel approach to signal reconstruction, leveraging the fact that many natural images exhibit sparse characteristics. This approach involves using a non-orthogonal sampling matrix within a framework inspired by total variation, and we demonstrate its effectiveness through both theoretical analysis and numerical experiments. Additionally, we explore the potential of applying this method to signals that are not inherently sparse. The results indicate that our proposed method outperforms traditional reconstruction techniques in terms of both the number of required measurements and the quality of the reconstructed signals. Furthermore, we observe that our method is more resilient to missing data than its traditional counterparts. This study examines the complexities of implementing clinical guidelines, which are developed by healthcare professionals, and then summarized into shorter, simpler guidelines that can be easily computed. The challenges arise when these two aspects collide, as longer, more intricate guidelines often produce more accurate treatment recommendations, whereas the concise yet accurate guidelines are more practical for everyday clinical use. The main objective of this paper is to provide a mathematical framework for understanding the trade-offs between accuracy and simplicity in clinical guidelines, and to demonstrate how these considerations can be taken into account when selecting the most suitable guidelines for specific patients or situations. The paper employs a theoretical model to model the accuracy of a guideline under various conditions and to model the impact of model prediction errors on patient outcomes. The results of this analysis are then applied to a case study involving the treatment of patients with sepsis, and the findings are compared to those of existing research. The case study reveals that the proposed approach can lead to better patient outcomes, and highlights the importance of considering both accuracy and simplicity when implementing clinical guidelines in practice. The findings also underscore the need for developing more accurate, computationally-efficient models to support clinical decision-making. Ultimately, this research provides a theoretical foundation for understanding the complexities of clinical guidelines and their potential to improve patient outcomes. The main contribution of this paper lies in developing a novel approach to model the trade-offs between accuracy and simplicity in clinical guidelines, and in demonstrating the potential of this approach to enhance patient care. The findings of this research can be extended to other areas, including the development of clinical decision support systems, and the design of more effective clinical guidelines. We propose a novel approach to computing weighted Voronoi diagrams with site-specific preferences, referred to as stable-matching Voronoi diagrams. This method leverages the Gale-Shapley algorithm for stable matchings, allowing for efficient computation in O(n log n) time even in the presence of non-negative weights. Building upon this framework, we develop a more comprehensive algorithm for computing stable-matching Voronoi diagrams under arbitrary weights, employing a divide-and-conquer strategy that yields a computational time complexity of O(n^2 log n). Furthermore, we demonstrate the utility of our approach in designing efficient algorithms for problems related to image processing. Notably, we present a novel algorithm for image segmentation based on Voronoi diagrams with stable matchings, which exhibits superior performance compared to existing methods. This approach is particularly advantageous in its ability to handle large images efficiently, thanks to its computational efficiency and memory management capabilities. Notably, the proposed algorithm requires a working memory of O(n) bits, allowing for efficient processing on modern hardware. Ultimately, we validate the effectiveness of our approach through a series of experiments conducted on both synthetic and real-world images. Notably, the proposed algorithm outperforms existing methods in terms of both accuracy and computational efficiency. The concept of chirality holds significant importance in the Standard Model and particle physics in general. Unfortunately, chirality is often overlooked in the development of Feynman diagrams. The ChIL language is then translated into a format compatible with the popular Feynman diagram software package, SExpress, for further analysis and processing. The chirality-based framework is expected to significantly enhance the efficiency of Feynman diagram creation and facilitate a deeper understanding of particle interactions in the Standard Model. Furthermore, this approach can be extended to other models, potentially revealing novel insights into particle physics. This paper presents a novel application of the Maximum Entropy Principle to determine the metabolic fluxes of cell cultures in a controlled chemostat environment. The principle is utilized to determine the unknown metabolic rates by balancing the observed growth rates of the cell culture with the observed concentrations of the culture's intracellular components, leveraging the fact that the cell's internal state is influenced by the overall growth rate rather than the specific metabolic fluxes. The resulting system can be expressed as a set of polynomial equations, and we explore the use of numerical homotopy continuation to solve this system, providing numerical examples and demonstrating the potential for generalization to more complex scenarios. The paper also outlines the limitations of this approach and suggests avenues for future research. The accompanying supplementary material includes a MATLAB implementation of the proposed method. However, this comes with increased energy loss and beam emittance growth due to the beam's transverse oscillations. To overcome this limitation, a novel technique is proposed, utilizing a periodic array of permanent magnets to manipulate the beam's trajectory and maintain a constant or even decreasing transverse size as it passes through the magnets, allowing for higher plasma interaction lengths and potentially higher wakefield ratios than previously possible. Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have been shown to be effective in improving performance, but they often suffer from a significant limitation: the need for expert expansion. This involves increasing the number of experts during training to achieve better results, which can be computationally costly and impractical. To address this issue, we introduce a novel technique called Gating Dropout, which enables MoE models to learn more efficiently and accurately without the need for expansion. This approach involves randomly disabling certain components of the model, including experts and parameters, during training to simulate the effect of having multiple experts. Unlike traditional methods, Gating Dropout considers the nature of the weight distribution within the model, which is typically Gaussian, and incorporates a gating mechanism to effectively mimic the behavior of multiple experts. This allows MoE models to achieve comparable performance levels without the need for expansion, and can even be used in conjunction with existing expansion methods to further improve performance. Experimental results demonstrate that Gating Dropout can lead to substantial performance gains, including a 4.5% increase in accuracy on the ImageNet dataset, and can be easily integrated into existing frameworks. The code and models can be accessed through our repository at https://github.com/THUMLP/Gating-Dropout. Additionally, we have conducted an in-depth analysis of the model's behavior and its implications for understanding the behavior of MoE models. The findings of this study are presented in a companion paper titled "Understanding MoE via Gating-Dropout". Both papers and the code will be publicly available upon publication. Graph neural networks (GNNs) have become a leading approach for graph representation learning. However, their ability to scale up is severely constrained by the computational cost of repeated message passing operations. This limitation becomes particularly pronounced when handling large-scale graphs that require extensive computations. To address this issue, we introduce a novel framework called GNNFlow that leverages the principles of flow networks to optimize GNN computations. By modeling GNNs as flow networks and leveraging network flow optimization techniques, GNNFlow efficiently minimizes message passing operations. This approach allows GNNFlow to handle larger graphs more effectively and accelerate training times. Through comprehensive experiments on multiple benchmark datasets, we demonstrate that GNNFlow outperforms existing GNN accelerators, achieving a significant training time reduction of up to 3.5x. We have conducted a comprehensive analysis of the orbits of planets in the TESS-Encrypted Catalog, which comprises 1,672 planets with known orbital periods. Our research reveals that the eccentricity distribution of these planets is consistent with a single Gaussian distribution, with a mean eccentricity of approximately 0.42 and a standard deviation of 0.16. Notably, we find that planets in systems with wide brown dwarf companions exhibit significantly higher eccentricities, particularly those with semi-major axes greater than 5 astronomical units. Our results also suggest that the eccentricities of these planets are predominantly influenced by the presence of a wide companion rather than the star's mass or multiplicity. Furthermore, we observe that planets in close binary systems tend to have lower eccentricities, which may be attributed to the suppression of eccentricity growth by the close companion. Our findings offer valuable insights into the formation mechanisms of planetary systems and their potential connections to the presence of wide brown dwarf companions. Ultimately, our study contributes to our understanding of the eccentricities of planetary systems and their dependence on the characteristics of the host stars and surrounding environment. These findings also hold significant implications for the study of exoplanetary atmospheres and the potential for future atmospheric characterization. Accurate stellar characteristics are essential for advancing the fields of stellar and exoplanetary science. To address this requirement, the Gaia mission will provide valuable data on stars, including their parallax, radial velocity, and proper motion. Nevertheless, precise stellar properties necessitate accounting for systematic errors in Gaia's astrometric data. To this end, we have developed a novel method for determining stellar ages, which incorporates Gaia's astrometric and photometric information, as well as spectroscopic data. This approach is capable of identifying stars with anomalous Gaia parallaxes, thereby enabling the detection of binary stars and other objects with uncertain distances. We have tested our method on a sample of 1000 stars with Gaia parallax uncertainties of less than 10%, as well as a subset of stars with anomalous Gaia parallaxes. The results indicate that our method can accurately determine ages for these stars, with a precision of 0.1-0.2 dex and a systematic offset of 0.05-0.1 dex, respectively. Furthermore, we have demonstrated that our method can be used to identify binary stars and to determine the masses of these systems. Ultimately, our approach can be applied to large datasets from Gaia, thereby facilitating the discovery of new stellar populations and the characterization of their properties. This research has significant implications for the development of more accurate stellar models, which are essential for understanding the evolution of stars and the formation of planetary systems. We examine a decentralized approach to training linear and kernel-based support vector machines. By adapting the Arrow-Debreu liquidation price model to the distributed setting, a primal-dual gradient algorithm is derived, which converges to the unique solution of the associated saddle-point formulation. This algorithm is then analyzed in the context of two decentralized SVM algorithms, one utilizing a convex combination of local loss functions and the other employing a weighted kernel estimate. We demonstrate the algorithm's convergence to the optimal solution using Lyapunov's stability theory and tools from convex analysis, and establish its convergence rate through a Lyapunov functional method. Specifically, we show that the algorithm converges at a rate of O(1/n^2) for the local loss function approach and O(1/n) for the weighted kernel estimate method, where n denotes the number of agents. To accurately detect disks using high-resolution polarized light images, we must consider the disk's inclination and distance from the observer. In this research, we investigate how the inclination and distance affect the visibility of these disks and how the disk's brightness and gas-to-dust ratio influence the observed polarized light levels. We used radiative transfer simulations to model circumplanetary disks and polarized scattered light observations. Our findings indicate that disks around gas giants are visible in polarized images up to 10-20 astronomical units away from the observer, and this distance is reduced to 2-3 times the disk's radius when the observer is at a 45-degree angle. Current operational systems for retrieving ocean dynamics from satellite altimeter data are mainly based on statistical methods, which are limited in their ability to capture the complex patterns of ocean circulation. A novel approach to this challenge is presented in this study, where a physics-based neural network (PhysNet) is utilized to create high-resolution, time-dependent maps of ocean velocity fields from altimeter data. In this study, PhysNet is applied to retrieve ocean velocity fields in the South China Sea, and the results show that it can accurately capture the complex patterns of ocean circulation and produce reliable predictions of ocean velocity. The results also show that PhysNet can significantly improve the accuracy of ocean velocity retrievals, especially for mesoscale features, by up to 30%, compared to current operational systems. The findings of this study highlight the potential of physics-based neural networks in retrieving ocean velocity fields from altimeter data and demonstrate their potential as a powerful tool for monitoring ocean circulation and climate change. The results of this study also provide valuable insights into the potential applications of neural networks in ocean remote sensing and climate change research. We investigate the computational complexity of the satisfiability problem for a propositional logic variant called IUL, which extends classical propositional logic with a universal modality. This logic variant is particularly useful for modeling infinite-state systems with unbounded data storage. Our research focuses on the model checking problem for IUL formulas within specific contexts: all formulas can be evaluated in polynomial time, and formulas with one variable have polynomial time complexity, while formulas with two variables have P-completeness. Additionally, we examine the model checking problem for IUL formulas in finite-state systems and establish lower and upper bounds. Specifically, we show that this problem is logspace-hard and within Logspace. Our findings are crucial for determining the computational complexity of checking IUL formulas in systems with bounded and unbounded storage. Our results also imply that the model checking problem for the sublass of IUL without the universal modality has a lower complexity, specifically coNP-hardness. Lastly, we discuss the implications of our findings on the decidability of the model checking problem for IUL. This research is part of a broader investigation into the computational complexity of the model checking problem for IUL. The results presented here are part of a larger study that will be published separately. The proofs of our claims rely on the application of advanced techniques in finite-state systems and the use of a new method for analyzing formulas with two variables. This new method is a valuable contribution to the study of the computational complexity of the model checking problem for IUL. Our results are also applicable to the study of the model checking problem for the subclass of IUL without the universal modality. This note provides an alternative demonstration of the $\alpha$-$\H^\times$-bounded calculus, originally developed by Hashimoto. The alternative proof is founded on recent advancements in the study of maximal regularity within asymptotically Hilbert spaces. Specifically, this new approach relies on a maximal $L_p$-regularity theorem achieved by Liu and Van Neerden in the context of Banach spaces. The existing proof of the $\alpha$-$\H^\times$-bounded calculus, as found in [7], heavily relies on a vector-valued Fourier multiplier theorem proven by a team of authors, [6]. We introduce a novel teleoperation system that enables robots to perform various tasks using real-time RGB-D camera feedback. The system allows humans to control a robot's end-effector to manipulate objects, leveraging the camera's 3D perception capabilities. We've developed an innovative teleoperation architecture that enables seamless execution of tasks that rely on spatial awareness, such as assembling objects, pouring liquids, and arranging items. The system's architecture consists of three core components: a teleoperation controller, a virtual end-effector controller, and a visual perception module. The teleoperation controller processes commands from a human operator, the virtual end-effector controller translates operator intent into precise robot actions, and the visual perception module provides the robot with essential 3D information. We've also developed a comprehensive simulation framework that allows for training and testing of the system. To validate the system's capabilities, we conducted a series of experiments, including a controlled study with human participants, and a robot-assisted assembly task. The results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in enabling robots to perform tasks that require spatial awareness, and highlight the potential of our system to expand robots' capabilities in human-robot collaboration. We introduce a measure of uncertainty for pairs of unitary operators, drawing inspiration from the concept of uncertainty associated with individual states. This measure is useful for characterizing uncertainty in quantum channels, particularly when they cannot be represented as the result of dephasing. Our findings indicate that when operators are compatible, the associated uncertainty vanishes, whereas uncertainty is maximized when operators are orthogonal. Additionally, we establish a relationship between the uncertainty of a channel and the degree of non-degeneracy of the associated unitary operator. This connection enables us to derive a lower bound for the uncertainty of a channel, drawing from the concept of non-degeneracy. Our work also yields a measure of uncertainty for channels that are not completely positive, leading to a new uncertainty bound for channels that are not trace-preserving. These results are further refined to apply to qubit channels, and numerical examples are provided to illustrate the validity of our uncertainty bounds. These findings have potential applications in the context of quantum error correction, particularly in the context of dephasing channels, and may also be relevant to the study of quantum channels that are not completely positive. Transformers have achieved remarkable success in computer vision tasks, particularly when processing long-range dependencies. However, their high computational cost and limited contextual reach make them less than ideal for dense feature extraction. To address this challenge, we introduce TransformerBlockNet (TBN), a novel network architecture that combines the strengths of Transformers and traditional convolutional neural networks. By integrating convolutional blocks with Transformers, TBN allows for the efficient extraction of dense features across multiple scales. Additionally, our proposed Pyramid Transformer (PyT) module enhances the network's ability to capture multi-scale dependencies and aggregate features effectively. Through extensive experimentation on various vision tasks, our TBN framework has demonstrated its versatility and competitive performance, outperforming state-of-the-art models in dense feature extraction. To analyze the impact of targeted online messages on public opinion formation during election campaigns, we developed a dynamic model that simulates how opinions evolve among interconnected individuals exposed to influence via social media. The model's parameters, including initial user opinions, are randomly reassessed in each iteration, allowing us to replicate a population's reaction to a series of social media messages. The resulting dataset is used to train a neural network that predicts the outcome of an election based on the social media text alone. To demonstrate the model's effectiveness, we applied it to a specific scenario - the 2016 U.S. presidential and French presidential elections - and found that it accurately predicted the election outcomes. Furthermore, we employed our model to investigate the influence of social media on public opinion, simulating various scenarios, such as an opponent countering an incumbent's tweets and an external actor attempting to sway the electorate. The results indicate that targeted online messages can significantly affect election outcomes, highlighting the need for effective regulation of social media. The accuracy of grammar correction systems is typically evaluated using automated metrics, but these tools do not account for the significance of specific grammatical errors in real-world applications. To address this limitation, we conducted a human evaluation of 1,000 grammatical errors across eight categories, with the results showing varying levels of perceived importance. For instance, subject-verb agreement errors were considered critical by 73% of the participants, while dative alternation mistakes were deemed insignificant by 82%. These findings can be used to develop more effective evaluation methods that prioritize the most significant errors. Furthermore, our research highlights the differences in opinions among human evaluators, with the majority agreeing that only specific types of grammatical errors are crucial for real-world applications. To this end, we propose a new evaluation framework that takes into account the varying significance of grammatical errors, with the ultimate goal of improving the evaluation of grammar correction systems. The mass-observable relation is a crucial component in the analysis of galaxy clusters, as it is necessary for deriving constraints on cosmology. However, the current mass-observable relation is insufficiently accurate, particularly in the context of future surveys. To address this limitation, we have developed a new parametrization of the mass-observable relation, which is based on the analysis of simulated cluster data. By utilizing this parametrization, we have been able to derive a more accurate relationship between galaxy cluster mass and X-ray luminosity, X-ray pressure profile, and thermal Sunyaev-Zel'dovich effect. Specifically, we have obtained a more precise relationship between galaxy cluster mass and X-ray luminosity, which is expressed as $M_{500} = \log_{10} M_{500} + A + B \log_{10} L_{500}$. The parameters $A$ and $B$ have been determined to be $A = 14.06 \pm 0.06$ and $B = 1.78 \pm 0.05$ for a redshift range of $0.1 \leq z \leq 3$. Furthermore, we have demonstrated that our parametrization is capable of accurately predicting the mass of galaxy clusters with an uncertainty of $\sim 10\%$. This improvement in accuracy is expected to significantly enhance the precision of cosmological constraints derived from galaxy clusters, particularly in the context of future surveys. Ultimately, the development of this parametrization is anticipated to contribute to the advancement of galaxy cluster cosmology. This model incorporates various production mechanisms, including the excitation of the target nucleus to a higher energy state, the excitation of the target nucleus to an isospin T=3/2 state via the exchange of a rho-meson, and the direct production of the K1(1270) via the exchange of a pi+ and pi- meson. Calculating shortest distances between graph nodes is a fundamental operation in many fields, including social network analysis and web search engines, but existing methods face scalability issues on large networks. To address this problem, we've developed a new data structure called HSSU that efficiently stores and processes graphs with billions of edges and nodes. By utilizing a novel algorithm based on the Bellman-Ford approach, our method outperforms current solutions and can be adapted to handle weighted and directed graphs. Additionally, our algorithm can be further optimized by employing a heuristic technique known as dynamic edge pruning, which significantly reduces computational time without compromising accuracy. Experimental results demonstrate the superior performance of our method compared to other leading techniques. Deep learning inference and pre-training tasks are increasingly resource-intensive, driving the need for a collaborative edge/cloud architecture that can efficiently process these tasks across distributed devices.  A key challenge in such systems is optimizing the allocation of tasks to ensure balanced load distribution across devices.  This paper presents a novel algorithm, DeepCluster, which leverages a clustering approach to group devices based on their capabilities, thereby enabling optimal task allocation and load balancing.  By dynamically grouping devices with similar capabilities, DeepCluster minimizes the likelihood of resource bottlenecks, ensuring efficient task execution and high-quality results.  Our experiments, conducted on a large-scale dataset of 100 devices, demonstrate the efficacy of DeepCluster in achieving a 30% reduction in completion time and 20% reduction in energy consumption, while maintaining a 0.5% accuracy difference compared to existing methods.  This work provides a theoretical foundation for task allocation in distributed deep learning systems, paving the way for future research in this area. This approach not only strengthens model robustness but also reduces its vulnerability to neuron failures and cyber threats. Ultimately, our results highlight the potential of multitask learning as a powerful tool for enhancing the robustness of neural language models. A novel model predictive control strategy is presented in this paper to optimize the speed and spacing of connected vehicles in highway platoons, addressing the challenges of state constraints and intervehicle communication delays. This proposed control scheme is an extension of Cooperative Adaptive Cruise Control and is formulated within a tube-based framework that accounts for uncertainties in intervehicle time delays. To mitigate the effects of communication time delays, the control strategy incorporates a predictive state estimator that takes into account the time delays between vehicles. Numerical simulations are used to demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed strategy. Compared to existing control methods, the results show that this strategy is effective in maintaining uniform vehicle headways and preventing collisions. Additionally, the proposed strategy is shown to be robust against time delays and can effectively mitigate the effects of communication failures. This makes it suitable for real-world highway platoon applications. The widespread use of digital devices has led to the degradation of numerous images, prompting the development of image restoration techniques. These techniques have largely focused on improving image quality through various methods, such as deblurring and noise removal. However, the existing literature lacks a comprehensive understanding of the potential of image restoration. To address this gap, we introduce a novel concept, image restoration potential, which assesses the level of restoration difficulty in an image and its sensitivity to noise. By defining this potential, we can enhance the effectiveness of image restoration algorithms. To this end, we propose a model that predicts image restoration potential using a combination of a feature extraction network and a lightweight network. The feature extraction network captures the image's structural features, while the lightweight network captures texture information. The extracted features are then combined and fed into a fully connected layer to calculate the image restoration potential. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of our proposed method in predicting image restoration potential compared to existing techniques. Furthermore, we show that our approach can be used to improve the performance of image restoration algorithms. The code and models are available for download on GitHub. We demonstrate that due to this interdependence, any attempt to control both wave characteristics results in a conflict between measurement control and the Heisenberg uncertainty relation. We introduce a novel statistical framework for analyzing brain connectivity patterns using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data, accounting for individual variability and noise in data measurements. Our approach involves modeling individual differences through a mixed-effects model, where population-wide fMRI connectivity patterns are estimated by separating individual differences from data variations caused by measurement noise. By incorporating a novel mixed-effects model within a Bayesian framework, we can accurately estimate the population-wide fMRI connectivity network, even with unbalanced datasets or noisy data measurements. Our method is demonstrated to provide reliable results in simulated data experiments, as well as in applications such as brain development, fMRI connectivity phenotypes, and neuroimaging studies. Specifically, we utilize our approach to examine the growth patterns of the human brain across different gestational ages, leveraging the advantages of our mixed-effects model. Moreover, we apply our method to detect resting-state fMRI connectivity phenotypes in patients with Alzheimer's disease, leveraging the power of our mixed-effects model for accurate phenotyping. The development of advanced reinforcement learning systems has sparked concerns about their ability to function as expected when given a perfect prediction system. In particular, this paper focuses on whether these agents can still make decisions based on their initial reward objectives even when their environments change significantly. In this context, three different scenarios are examined to determine under what conditions these agents would continue to act in their intended way. Surprisingly, even with the most basic of models, it's found that there's a high likelihood of the agent becoming stuck in a suboptimal state. This raises serious questions about the safety of using such sophisticated technologies in real-world applications. In an effort to mitigate these risks, this paper proposes a novel approach to ensure that agents remain aligned with their intended reward objectives. The method involves creating a model that can predict the agent's behavior and then using it to refine the agent's decision-making process. The results of using this approach on a range of challenging tasks show that it's possible to ensure the agent's safety and align it with its intended goals. The code used in this research is publicly available on GitHub. Music streaming platforms provide users with three main ways to access content: listening to radio stations, browsing through categorized sections and searching for specific tracks or artists. While radio stations and browsing offer an unsupervised experience, search functionality allows users to explore music by actively seeking out particular songs or albums. This research focuses on how users utilize search to discover new music, examining search queries and the associated user behavior and music consumption patterns. We conducted a comprehensive analysis of search queries and user behavior data from a leading music streaming service, applying various text analysis techniques to identify patterns in search behavior. Our findings reveal that users primarily utilize search to investigate particular songs or artists, often searching for music that matches a specific mood or style. Additionally, we discovered that users can be broadly categorized into three main categories: those who search for specific tracks, those who search for music related to a particular mood or style, and those who search for general information. These categories are associated with distinct patterns of music consumption. Our research provides valuable insights for improving music recommendation systems, particularly in the context of search functionality. We propose a novel approach to music recommendation that takes into account the user's search history and provides tailored suggestions for future searches. This approach is designed to enhance the overall search experience and provide users with more accurate and relevant music recommendations. We believe that this research has the potential to contribute significantly to the development of advanced music recommendation systems. This study investigates the phenomenon of semantically equivalent tokens that cause little or no impact on translation performance in standard WMT tasks, yet become sources of attack for adversarial methods. Based on our findings, we propose a new and efficient adversarial training approach that builds on iterative gradient projection attacks, but improves upon them by incorporating semantic analysis to filter out ineffective tokens. The results of our experiments demonstrate that this approach can enhance the robustness of NMT models against various types of attacks. Multiple Imputation is a widely employed technique for addressing missing data in self-reported questionnaires and surveys. However, the current methods for this technique fail to account for the complexities of data that are often subject to change over time and space. Existing algorithms for generating models within the MI framework are limited in their ability to capture these spatio-temporal dynamics. This research focuses on the spread of the novel COVID-19 virus in Algeria from March 14th, 2020, to May 24th, 2020. Initially, a susceptible-infected-recovered (SIR) model was employed to model the spread, and the estimated basic reproduction number (R0) was found to be 3.35 on March 14th, 2020. Notably, the mean absolute error (MAE) for infected cases was 11.35, and for deceased cases, it was 4.34. These findings align with the reality that the mortality rate of COVID-19 is significantly lower than that of other infectious diseases such as Ebola. Consequently, the SIR model's performance is compromised by underestimating the number of infected individuals and overestimating the number of recovered individuals. To address this, the research also explored the application of a deep learning model to forecast infected and deceased individuals, and the results were compared to those of the SIR model. Ultimately, the deep learning approach proved to be more accurate in predicting the spread of COVID-19 in Algeria compared to the SIR model. This research's findings have the potential to inform policymakers in developing effective strategies to mitigate the impact of future outbreaks. Deep learning models have been increasingly applied to address the long-standing issue of software traceability, where features extracted by these models can facilitate the prediction of relevant traces for given entities, such as requirements and source code. However, existing deep learning trace models are limited by their inability to provide insights into why a particular trace is recommended, making it difficult to identify the key factors driving the recommendation. This paper proposes a novel attention-based model, called TraceBert, which leverages the capabilities of the BERT model to extract informative features from software development data and provide transparent explanations for trace recommendations. Experimental results demonstrate the superior performance of TraceBert compared to existing state-of-the-art methods, as well as its ability to offer understandable explanations for its predictions. A case study further validates the effectiveness of the proposed approach in uncovering the underlying reasons for its recommendations. This work aims to explore the possibility of applying the principles of conformal quantum mechanics to the Bianchi type III cosmology, a specific variant that is characterized by spatial homogeneity but non-isotropic metric. By employing the Dirac field as our quantum probe, we are able to derive a Hamiltonian that governs the field's evolution within this particular cosmological framework. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the Bianchi type III cosmology can be effectively described in terms of a particle moving in a curved space, a finding that is reminiscent of the quantum mechanics of non-relativistic particles in curved spacetime. Notably, our approach yields a novel expression for the universe's expansion rate, which is distinct from the conventional Friedmann equation. This work represents a pioneering effort in the application of conformal quantum mechanics to the Bianchi cosmologies, and its findings are expected to provide valuable insights into the nature of quantum cosmology. Ultimately, our research aims to shed light on the quantum properties of the universe and its evolution, particularly in the context of the early cosmos. Recent breakthroughs in neural generation models have led to the development of sophisticated text generators. Despite these advancements, these models often struggle to produce coherent and meaningful text when entities are involved. To address this challenge, we introduce a novel neural approach that incorporates entity information into the generation process. By combining a language model with an entity-aware component that captures local entity interactions, our method effectively guides the generation process. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach significantly improves the quality of generated text, particularly in entity-related applications such as question answering. Furthermore, our entity-enhanced model can be seamlessly integrated into existing neural generators to enhance their performance. To facilitate further research, we release our code and entity-enhanced data sets on the GitHub platform at https://github.com/IBM/ERLM. Smart contracts are small yet complex programs deployed on blockchain networks, 
offering automated transactions and enabling decentralized, peer-to-peer exchange of assets. 
The complexity and compact nature of these contracts make them prone to static analysis, 
but dynamic analysis is often hindered by the difficulty of generating test scenarios. 
This paper introduces Smartester, a tool designed to facilitate dynamic analysis of smart contracts. 
By leveraging genetic programming and mutation testing techniques, Smartoster generates test cases 
using the Solidity programming language, aiming to detect errors, validate correct code, and identify untested execution paths. 
The tool's effectiveness is demonstrated through a series of case studies, in which Smartoster uncovered 
several previously unknown bugs in established smart contracts. 
The results indicate that Smartoster is a valuable asset for dynamic analysis and testing of smart contracts.

In ecommerce, sponsored search plays a significant role in facilitating discovery of products to users. However, the effectiveness of sponsored search can be compromised when ads appear unexpectedly, disrupting user interactions. To address this challenge, we propose an innovative approach that integrates the sponsored search placement model with the bidding system, aiming to strike a balance between relevant ads and user experience. Our experiments on a large ecommerce dataset demonstrate substantial improvements in user interactions, with a significant increase in total clicks and cost-per-click. Moreover, our approach ensures that the search visibility remains within predetermined limits. Go's design, centered around coroutines and channels, enables seamless parallel processing in user-space applications, potentially bypassing kernel limitations. We developed the LiteVM, a lightweight virtual machine that translates Go code into efficient, parallelized C functions. By utilizing a unique, thread-local heap and optimized memory management, LiteVM significantly reduces memory usage and nears the performance of real Go programs, particularly for short-running programs. Our results demonstrate that LiteVM can effectively execute Go functions in user-space C programs, achieving substantial memory savings with minimal lost performance. The LiteVM source code is available for review.

The main goal of High-Level Synthesis is to automatically generate Hardware Description Language code from behavioral descriptions.  However, existing tools struggle to achieve significant speedups, largely due to their inability to effectively utilize parallelization techniques.  This limitation stems from the fact that most parallelization approaches were designed for software development and are not well-suited for the unique characteristics of Hardware Description Language.  To address this issue, we propose a new framework for parallelizing loops in Hardware Description Language, which leverages a combination of static and dynamic methods to improve the performance of pipelined and parallel loops.  Experimental results demonstrate that our framework can significantly accelerate the execution of both pipelized and parallel functions, with some examples achieving a 3.6 and 2.8-fold speedup, respectively, compared to optimized C implementations on a Xilinx ZC706 FPGA.  Furthermore, our framework can also be applied to optimize the performance of systems consisting of multiple loops.  In these cases, our approach can deliver a substantial speedup of 3.2 times the speed of a baseline system, while maintaining a high degree of resource efficiency.  To facilitate the reproducibility of our findings, we have made the relevant source code available on GitHub.  This includes a publicly accessible repository containing the optimized C code, SystemC-TLM models, and hardware implementations for the benchmarked functions, as well as a detailed description of our experimental methodology.  This repository can be accessed at the following location: https://github.com/ParLoC-UC3M/ParLoC.  Finally, we have also made the relevant tools and libraries used in our experiments publicly available, including the VizPipelined and VizParLoC tools, which provide a visual representation of pipelined and parallel loops, respectively.  These tools can be accessed at the following location: https://github.com/ParLoC-UC3M/VizPipelined and https://github.com/ParLoC-UC3M/VizParLoC.  The source code for these tools is included in the repository. In microfluidic systems, the movement of solutes is influenced by a complex interplay of forces, including diffusion, convection, and buoyancy. While diffusion and convection are well-understood, the effect of buoyancy is often overlooked, particularly in devices that operate at a large scale compared to the solute size. In this research, we investigate the impact of buoyancy on the microdiffusion of a single solute in a square channel with a slight tilt, using both analytical and numerical approaches. Our findings reveal that the combination of diffusion and convection caused by the tilt leads to a periodic oscillation in the solute concentration at the channel outlet, which can be precisely controlled by adjusting the tilt angle. This discovery offers a novel method for measuring the diffusion coefficient of a solute, eliminating the need for complex calibration procedures. Furthermore, the findings of this study can be applied to develop a microfluidic device that enables the controlled release of a solute from a microchannel, which can have significant implications for drug delivery systems. This paper presents a novel approach to efficiently sampling multidimensional mixing distributions, which are a critical component of mixture models. The conventional method for sampling from such distributions relies on the Monte Carlo method, utilizing quadrature to approximate high-dimensional integrals. However, its effectiveness is severely limited by the square root of the number of dimensions, hindering its application in high-dimensional settings. To overcome this limitation, we introduce a new Monte Carlo algorithm that employs a novel variance-reducing technique, which we demonstrate to be universally applicable across all mixing distributions, and experimentally verify to be superior to existing approaches in various scenarios. The proposed algorithm is also integrated into a Markov chain Monte Carlo framework, which we apply to estimate the parameters of a spatial generalized linear model. The results of our numerical experiments demonstrate the superior efficiency of our approach in comparison to established alternatives. Finally, we apply the proposed method to estimate the parameters of a spatial generalized linear model using data from the US housing market. camera positions. To address this, we suggest leveraging information from existing
camera positions to accurately forecast the arrangement of external viewpoints.

views in a complex environment, which we test and evaluate against established
optimization techniques in simulated and real-world scenarios. Our results show
that the network effectively estimates camera views in a variety of settings,
including simple rooms and large outdoor scenes. Notably, we demonstrate that
the network's predictions enable the recovery of 3D reconstructions without the
need for bundle adjustment. This approach has the potential to accelerate the
Structure-from-Motion process, making it more efficient. The associated code and

High-energy X-ray scattering techniques are particularly well-suited to study
superionic states, which are unique mix of solid and liquid properties.
These techniques enable researchers to measure the diffuse scattering of
ions in highly mobile liquids, ultimately revealing the atomic structure
within the material. This review highlights the significance of diffuse scattering
in the atomic structure of superionic conductors and showcases the capabilities
of modern high-energy X-ray facilities in analyzing this phenomenon.
Specifically, we will delve into the case of superionic silver chalcogenides,
examine the findings from high-resolution diffuse scattering experiments, and
outline the key findings. These findings will be contextualized within the
existing body of knowledge on the structural characteristics of these materials. 
Finally, we will discuss the potential of future high-performance X-ray
facilities, such as the European X-ray Free Electron Laser Facility (EU-XFEL) 
and the Advanced Photon Source (APS), in advancing our understanding of
superionic materials.

This concise document provides an overview of the Gumbel-max trick, a crucial technique in various applications within machine learning, such as sampling from complex distributions and Bayesian methods. The accompanying code is included in the form of a Python implementation utilizing the NumPy library. The explanation assumes familiarity with concepts such as categorical distributions, log probabilities, and vector operations. 

**Sample Use Cases**

The Gumbel-max approach has practical applications in two main areas:

1. **Sampling from a categorical distribution**: This can be achieved by generating Gumbel samples for multiple components, then ranking and selecting the highest-ranked sample, effectively sampling from a distribution where $p_i = \exp(p_i)$. 

2. **Approximating Bayesian inference**: This can be achieved by generating samples from a conditional distribution where $p(y|X) = \exp(p(y|X))$. 

**Python Implementation**

```python
import numpy as np

def gumbel_sample(n, eps=1e-20):
    return np.random.gumbel(size=n) + eps

def gumbel_max(e, gumbel):
    indices = np.argsort(e + gumbel)
    return indices[-1] if len(indices) == 1 else indices[-len(indices):] - len(indices)

def sample_categorical(probs, num_samples=1):
    log_probs = np.log(probs)
    gumbel_samples = gumbel_sample(len(probs), eps=1e-20)
    ranked_samples = gumbel_max(e=log_probs, gumbel=gumbel_samples)
    return np.exp(probs[ranked_samples])

# Example usage
num_classes = 5
probabilities = np.random.rand(num_classes)
gumbel_samples = gumbel_sample(n=100, eps=1e-20)
sampled_probabilities = sample_categorical(probs=probabilities, num_samples=100)
print("Sampled Probabilities: ", sampled_probabilities)
```

We establish a method for estimating average indirect effects of a binary intervention. This intervention influences an outcome either directly or indirectly, through a mediator, and the treatment's impact on the mediator is linear and known. Leveraging this insight, we develop an identification equation that represents the total indirect effect as a combination of the treatment's influence on the mediator and the mediator's influence on the outcome. The results show that the certification indeed influences the teacher's instructional practices, leading to improved student performance. Notably, we found that the certification effects operate primarily through these practices, and the confidence interval is distinct from zero. Researchers have developed various techniques to counter ML attacks, yet there's a lack of standardization in the way these studies are conducted. This lack of standardization makes it difficult to compare and build upon existing research, hindering the reproducibility of results. This, in turn, poses a significant challenge to the validity of cybersecurity studies, as unverifiable assumptions can lead to unreliable conclusions. To address this issue, we propose a framework for documenting and sharing research data sets in the context of ML attack evaluation. By utilizing a structured approach to represent datasets, we aim to enhance the reproducibility and reusability of research findings, ultimately facilitating the sharing of knowledge within the ML security community. Our methodology is demonstrated through a case study on black-box attacks against image classifiers. To further illustrate the practicality of our approach, we provide a real-world example of a dataset used in the evaluation of adversarial attacks, showcasing its potential for enhancing the reproducibility of research and the sharing of knowledge within the ML security field. By making datasets more easily comparable and combinable, we can accelerate the advancement of cybersecurity research. We propose a novel approach, Reinforced Assembly Generation (RAG), which leverages Reinforcement Learning to automatically create desired spatial arrangements of particles. By defining a goal condition through a reward function, RAG generates particles' positions without requiring pre-established configurations. Our method is grounded in the particle-based simulation technique, with the goal of optimizing particle positions based on a target density field. To achieve this, we developed a reward function that penalizes particles' deviations from their desired positions. To validate our approach, we conducted a series of experiments with various reward function designs, including those based on density fields, pairwise potentials, and pairwise density rewards. Ultimately, we demonstrated the effectiveness of RAG in generating complex particle arrangements that meet specific criteria in a few hundred iterations, with the added benefit of adaptability to diverse reward function designs. The primary objective of monocular 3D object detection is to identify 3D bounding boxes in images without relying on additional depth information. Most existing methods utilize depth maps as input, which are typically estimated using stereo matching techniques that can be computationally expensive. In contrast, our approach leverages the depth information inherent in the image itself by incorporating a depth-aware image encoder. This encoder is trained end-to-end alongside a regression head, which predicts 3D bounding boxes directly from image features. Notably, our method is the first to achieve state-of-the-art results without requiring estimated depth maps and can even operate without access to depth information. When trained on KITTI and evaluated on the same dataset, our method surpasses the performance of KITTI 3D detectors, and when trained on the larger nuScenes dataset and then evaluated on KITTI, our method achieves the highest accuracy among monocular 3D detectors. Moreover, our method is the first to be trained and evaluated on the full KITTI and nuScenes datasets without access to ground truth depth maps. The code and pre-trained models are publicly available on the GitHub repository. https://github.com/yourname/monodepth3d. We also provide a live demo at https://monodepth3d.github.io. Brain gliomas are the most common brain cancer type and pose a significant challenge in clinical diagnosis. Combining multiple MRI modalities, including anatomical and functional information, has been shown to improve diagnostic accuracy. However, extracting and utilizing spatial-temporal features from these modalities remains a significant hurdle. This paper proposes a novel deep learning approach that leverages spatial-temporal features from multi-modal MRI scans to classify brain gliomas. The approach involves a two-stage process: the first stage extracts spatial-temporal features from MRI scans using a convolutional neural network, and the second stage utilizes a graph convolutional network to integrate local and global spatial-temporal information. The approach is validated through experiments on two publicly available datasets, yielding superior results compared to existing methods. The proposed method achieves a significant improvement in classification accuracy, with a 4.4% increase in AUC and 5.6% in accuracy on the whole brain dataset, and a 3.1% increase in AUC and 4.5% in accuracy on the subcortical brain dataset. The development of neural network and physics-based models for programmable photonic chips is crucial for designing these components.  Currently available physics-based models are computationally intensive, limiting their practical use, whereas neural network-based models are computationally efficient but lack the transparency of the original physics-based models.  In this study, we introduce a novel approach to create interpretable neural network-based models for photonic chips by leveraging the insights gained from a simplified physics-based model.  This method enables the neural network model to effectively approximate the complex relationship between the photonic chip's architecture and its optical properties, while also providing a clear understanding of the original physics-based model.  Experimental results demonstrate the accuracy of the proposed method in terms of both performance and explainability.  This study's findings have the potential to facilitate the development of more accurate and transparent photonic chip design tools.  In addition, the proposed method can be extended to other physics-based machine learning applications. Software systems can be optimized by tailoring their runtime configuration to specific applications, thereby enhancing key performance characteristics such as file size, processing speed, and power consumption. However, this customization often requires significant manual effort and can be prone to errors. To address this challenge, we introduce an automated approach for optimizing software systems based on their performance profiles. This method leverages machine learning to identify the most effective configuration settings for each application under consideration. To validate the efficacy of our approach, we apply it to the widely used Apache HTTP Server, demonstrating that it can reduce the server's binary size by up to 44%, decrease its startup time by up 14%, and minimize memory usage by up to 23%. These optimizations result in an average improvement of up to 10% in web page delivery speed. Additionally, our approach is highly efficient, processing large-scale Apache configurations within a few seconds on a standard laptop. To further facilitate the adoption of our approach, we make our source code freely available to the research community. This method has the potential to be adapted for optimizing other software systems based on their performance profiles.
